title: Thinking About Interior and Exterior Angles (Part 1 of 3): Using Logo Programming to Explore Exterior Angles part-1-of-3-using-logo-programming-to-explore-exterior-angles/
author: Rowlandson, Paul
summary: Paul Rowlandson describes using turtle-graphics Logo programming to introduce exterior angles, building on his own memory of the concept "clicking" for him only when he had to program a robot to trace a triangle. Using free tools like Python Sandbox, he has students predict what angle a coded turtle needs to turn to trace a triangle, most of whom instinctively write 60 degrees, the interior angle, and are then surprised by the resulting shape when the code is run at that value. The productive confusion this generates drives paired discussion and repeated mini-whiteboard predictions until the class converges on the correct value of 120 degrees, after which Rowlandson explicitly names what students have implicitly discovered: the exterior angle is the angle the arrow turns through, and interior and exterior angles at a vertex sum to 180 degrees since together they form a straight line. He extends the activity to derive that exterior angles of any polygon sum to 360 degrees, using the visual fact that the turtle makes exactly one full turn by the time it returns to its starting orientation, and shows how this fact provides a shortcut for problems that would otherwise require first calculating an unknown interior angle.
points: Rowlandson's activity is deliberately built around a predictable misconception, students defaulting to the interior angle when asked for the turn, using the visible, animated mismatch as the mechanism that drives conceptual change rather than lecturing the distinction upfront.
His repeated-prediction structure (guess, watch, discuss, re-guess) mirrors a diagnostic-question cycle, using mini-whiteboards to make the whole class's evolving understanding visible at each stage.

The "exterior angles sum to 360 degrees" generalisation is derived visually, since the turtle makes exactly one full turn, rather than asserted, giving students a physical justification they can reconstruct rather than a fact to memorise.
He explicitly builds in physical embodiment, having a student stand up and re-enact the arrow's turns, as a second representation of the same abstract fact alongside the coded animation.
quotes: A time that I remember the concept of exterior angles really clicking for me as a student was when trying to program a turtle robot to move in a way that traces an equilateral triangle.
Naturally, most of the class wrote 60 on their mini-whiteboards and then expressed surprise when they watched the arrow draw this

They need to consider the angle that the arrow turns at each vertex. In other words, they need to imagine the line that the arrow would draw if it continued moving forward, look at the line they want the arrow to draw, and consider the angle between them.

I have found that setting the animations to ‘slow’ and allowing students to watch the arrow moving and turning gives them plenty of opportunities to see how it always starts and finishes pointing in the same direction.

Many students’ first instincts are often to calculate the two interior angles, calculate the missing interior angle, and then calculate its exterior angles. But they can then see how a quicker way would be to simply subtract the two exterior angles from 360 degrees instead.
